memory_candidates.content: When a known-failures.txt (or similar known-failing registry) row is claimed as a task's scope, re-run the named suite FIRST and diff its live [FAIL] text against the row's claimed symptom shape before trusting the row's prose. A row can be seeded after the defect it describes was already fixed by an unrelated commit, while the suite stays red for a later, different reason that happens to resemble the original symptom (same case numbers, same counter names). Scoping work from the row's text alone risks solving an already-solved problem while missing the suite's actual live failure.

To probe a bash test suite's resistance to a specific partial fix, do not always literally delete/comment the target lines -- under a harness using `set -u` (nounset), deleting an unconditional-reset block can crash the whole script with 'unbound variable' at the FIRST call site, before the targeted downstream assertion is ever reached, masking the intended signal. Instead simulate the fault's literal shape with an only-if-unset init (`: "${VAR:=0}"` instead of `VAR=0`) -- this reproduces 'stale state survives across calls' without ever leaving the variable unset, so execution reaches and fails the specific assertion the probe is meant to exercise.
